procedural_history.originating_court: Income Tax Officer (Section X Central) Bombay filed a complaint.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated October 18, 1968 of the Delhi High Court, Himachal Bench at Simla in Civil Writ No. 365 of 1968.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant, Advance Insurance Company Limited, filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in the Delhi High Court challenging the right of the Special Police Establishment to investigate the case. The High Court dismissed the petition on October 18, 1968.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court with a certificate granted by the High Court after the High Court dismissed their petition.

directions: There will be no order about costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Special Police Establishment has the right to investigate the case in Maharashtra State.

facts: A case was registered by the Special Police Establishment (SPE) in New Delhi for offences under sections 409 and 477A of the Indian Penal Code.
The investigation was to be conducted in the State of Maharashtra.
The appellant company challenged the right of the SPE to investigate the case in Maharashtra.
law: Under the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act of 1946, the SPE can exercise its powers and jurisdiction in a state only with the consent of that state's government.
The Central Government must also issue a notification specifying the offences that the SPE is empowered to investigate.
application: The Court found that a Central Government notification from November 6, 1956, had already empowered the SPE to investigate offences under sections 409 and 477-A of the Indian Penal Code.

The Court then identified a memorandum from July 2, 1960, which showed that the Government of Maharashtra had explicitly consented to the SPE exercising its powers and jurisdiction within Maharashtra for the very offences listed in the 1956 notification.
The Court noted that since consent had already been given for these specific offences, no fresh consent was necessary.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the challenge, holding that the Special Police Establishment had the right to investigate the case because the Government of Maharashtra had given the necessary consent for the SPE to investigate these specific offences within the state.

issue.issue_text: Whether the adaptation of the General Clauses Act in 1956 would be invalid because the time limit for such adaptations under Article 372(3) of the Constitution had expired in 1953.

facts: In 1956, the President issued the Adaptation of Laws (No. 1) Order, which amended the definition of 'State' in the General Clauses Act.
The appellant argued that this adaptation was invalid.
The basis for the appellant's argument was that the President's power to adapt laws under Article 372(2) of the Constitution had a time limit which expired in 1953.
law: The Court acknowledged that the President's power under Article 372(2) had indeed expired in 1953.
However, the Court identified a new provision, Article 372A, which was introduced into the Constitution by the Seventh Amendment Act of 1956.
Article 372A conferred a "fresh power equal and analogous" to the one in Article 372(2) on the President to adapt and modify laws to align them with the changes made by the Seventh Amendment.
application: The Court reasoned that the 1956 adaptation of the General Clauses Act was not made under the expired power of Article 372(2).
Instead, the adaptation was validly made under the new power granted to the President by Article 372A.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the 1956 adaptation of the General Clauses Act was valid because it was sustained by the fresh power conferred upon the President by the newly introduced Article 372A of the Constitution.

issue.issue_text: Whether the expression 'belonging to' in the relevant legal entry should be interpreted in a way that would render the scheme of investigation by an outside police force void.

facts: The appellants argued that the expression 'belonging to' should be interpreted as 'employed by' rather than just 'located in'.
Under this interpretation, the Special Police Establishment (SPE), whose superintendence vests in the Central Government, would not 'belong to' the Union Territory of Delhi.
The opposing argument was that 'belonging to' simply conveys a 'territorial nexus', meaning a police force constituted and functioning in a particular area.
law: The Court applied the principle of the presumption of constitutionality, stating that "Provisions of law must be read as far as is possible with a view to their validity and not to render them invalid."
application: The Court acknowledged that the words 'belonging to' were susceptible to the meaning suggested by the appellants.
However, since the words were also capable of the 'territorial nexus' meaning, the Court chose the interpretation that would uphold the validity of the legal scheme.
The Court defined the expression 'belonging to' as conveying "the meaning that it is 'a police force constituted and functioning in one area' which may be authorised to function in another area."
Applying this definition, the Court determined that the Delhi Special Police Establishment is a police force constituted and functioning in the Union Territory of Delhi.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's interpretation because it would have rendered the entire scheme invalid. Instead, it held that 'belonging to' signifies a territorial connection, meaning a police force constituted and functioning in a specific area. As the Delhi Special Police Establishment functioned in the Union Territory of Delhi, it 'belonged to' that territory for the purposes of the law, thus validating the scheme of investigation by an outside police force.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Special Police Establishment has the right to investigate the case in Maharashtra State.
appellant_arguments: The consent of the Government of Maharashtra was necessary for the newly added offences (ss. 409 and 477-A).
The consent of the Maharashtra government was not properly considered or given, and has not been proven.
respondent_arguments: The Maharashtra Government had consented on more than one occasion to the investigation of the offences in the State.
The new notification was merely a restatement of the old one, which included some other offences.
An affidavit from the Under Secretary to the Government of Maharashtra confirms that the Chief Minister had considered the matter and given his consent, which he was competent to do.
There is a presumption of regularity of official acts, and the memorandum and affidavit clearly establish that consent was given.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the adaptation of the General Clauses Act in 1956 would be invalid because the time limit for such adaptations under Article 372(3) of the Constitution had expired in 1953.
appellant_arguments: The power to adapt laws under Article 372(2) of the Constitution had a time limit of three years as per clause (3) of the article.
Therefore, the adaptation of the General Clauses Act in 1956 is invalid, and the definition prior to the amendment should apply.
respondent_arguments: The adaptation of the General Clauses Act in 1956 was valid under Article 372(2).

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Provisions of law must be read as far as is possible with a view to their validity and not to render them invalid.
obiter: There is a presumption of regularity of official acts.
So long as the words of a statute are capable of bearing a meaning that upholds its validity, it is not necessary to discover another meaning under which the scheme would become void.
The expression 'belonging to' conveys the meaning that it is a police force constituted and functioning in one area, which may be authorised to function in another area.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court dismissed the appeal, finding that the Special Police Establishment's investigation in Maharashtra was valid. The court determined that the state government had properly consented to the investigation, as evidenced by an official affidavit and supported by the presumption of regularity of official acts. Furthermore, the court interpreted the relevant legal provisions in a manner that would uphold the validity of the scheme allowing an outside police force to investigate, rather than adopting an interpretation that would render it void.
legal_tests_applied: Presumption of regularity of official acts.
Provisions of law must be read as far as is possible with a view to their validity and not to render them invalid.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument that consent was not properly given, finding that an affidavit from the Under Secretary of Maharashtra, stating the Chief Minister had given consent, was sufficient proof.

The court considered the new notification authorizing the investigation to be merely a restatement of a prior notification for which consent had already been given, not a request for new consent for old offences.
The court refused to go behind the official memorandum and affidavit presented as evidence of consent.

The court chose to interpret the ambiguous expression 'belonging to' in a way that upheld the validity of the law, stating that it is not necessary to discover another meaning under which the whole scheme would become void.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully established that the Maharashtra Government had consented to the investigation, which was confirmed by an affidavit from the Under Secretary.
The court applied the presumption of regularity of official acts to the memorandum and affidavit, concluding they clearly established that consent was given.

The court accepted the respondent's implicit position that the legal framework should be interpreted to be valid, holding that the expression 'belonging to' simply means a police force constituted in one area authorized to function in another.
policy_considerations: The court articulated a policy of judicial interpretation that favors the validity of laws, stating, 'Provisions of Jaw must be read as far as is possible with a view to their validity and not to render them invalid.'
